title: Lula wins Brazil’s election and thanks women. Delivering for them is the next test.
subtitle: Brazil’s electoral authority confirms a fourth term for Lula as Flávio Bolsonaro challenges the vote. Women’s place in the victory speech now gives way to questions about policy, access and accountability.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term as Brazil’s president, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in the 25 October runoff and singling out Brazilian women for their support as he celebrated the result.

The Superior Electoral Court’s update published early on 26 October put Lula at 51.79% of valid votes and Bolsonaro at 48.21%. The result gives the incumbent another term, but the political confrontation has not ended: Bolsonaro says he will seek to overturn the election.

In remarks reported by the Senate’s news service on election night, Lula said the affection he had received, particularly from Brazilian women, had exceeded anything he had imagined. That acknowledgement places women prominently in his account of the victory. It does not, on its own, establish how women voted or how much their support contributed to the winning margin.
What the result tells us—and what it does not

Before the runoff, women represented 52.84% of registered voters, according to the electoral court. Their numerical strength made them central to both campaigns. Yet an electorate containing millions of women across different incomes, religions and regions cannot be treated as a single political constituency.

A Datafolha survey conducted on 20–22 October had Lula ahead among women by 53% to 47% of valid voting intentions. It interviewed 2,520 voters overall, with a three-percentage-point margin of error for the gender groups. Those were pre-election estimates, not a count of ballots cast by women.

The official national tally confirms the winner. It does not reveal each voter’s choice by gender. Establishing women’s contribution more precisely requires credible post-election survey evidence, with its sampling and limitations disclosed. Neither a campaign’s gratitude nor the national result supplies that breakdown.

Turnout did improve. The electoral court reported that approximately 128.2 million people voted and that abstention fell to around 19.2%, from 21.08% in the first round. Those national figures do not establish which demographic groups accounted for the increase.
A dispute over access to the ballot

Bolsonaro told Reuters that he would not concede and would seek annulment, objecting to Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours. His announcement is a statement of intended legal action, not a judicial finding that the result is invalid.

The electoral court acknowledged operational difficulties. Its president, Kassio Nunes Marques, said the extension applied to polling stations still open, while machines already closed could not be reopened. Receiving polling-station results was temporarily suspended, creating a processing backlog.

The court nevertheless announced Lula’s victory. Explaining the administrative disruption and evaluating any legal challenge are distinct tasks; neither should be replaced by assuming that a delayed count demonstrates a fraudulent one.

For voters, the dispute also raises a practical question about equal access. A legal entitlement to vote depends on being able to reach a polling station and complete the process. Transport arrangements and opening hours deserve scrutiny as part of that access, alongside the accuracy of the count.
The promises now face a governing test

Lula’s next term will confront pressure on household budgets and public finances. Reuters reports that he plans further household-debt relief and that his team has pledged to retain the government’s budget rules. Bolsonaro’s party and its allies are set to control both chambers of Congress, complicating the president’s legislative agenda.

For women managing debt, earning a living or supporting relatives, the useful questions are concrete: who qualifies for assistance, how much relief reaches a household, and whether services remain accessible. A victory speech cannot answer those questions; programme rules, budgets and delivery records can.

During the campaign, Lula also promised gender-equality lessons in schools, according to a September analysis by Americas Quarterly. That remains a policy commitment to examine, rather than an outcome the election has delivered. Its significance would depend on what is taught, how teachers are prepared and whether implementation survives political resistance.

Women who supported Lula, women who chose Bolsonaro and women who rejected both remain entitled to public services and accountable government. The election decides who takes responsibility for governing them all.

Lula has publicly recognised women in his victory. The measure of that recognition will be whether they can identify improvements in their safety, financial security and opportunities—and hold his government to account when promises are not fulfilled.
The Athena Perspective.
